cards.title: From Paper to Card: Transforming Design Implications with Generative AI
cards.meta: CHI 2024 · doi 10.1145/3613904.3642266 · comparison only, zero credit

rows.value: The lineage is a cited chain of eliminations ending at the machine. Cited work establishes that design implications as written in papers are rarely read or used and that designers find the papers jargon-filled and unhelpful, and cites the resulting calls for translational resources. Design cards are cited as the established format with a long tradition. Each way of producing them is then cited and ruled out: researchers are cited as lacking time, incentive and the skill to make a card inspiring, and a crowd approach, cited from a project that made videos of research talks, is cited as giving patchy and biased coverage. The evaluation is the most load-bearing citation of all: six criteria for judging a design implication, taken whole from one cited paper, become the survey's six scales, with the cited claim that three of them measure utility and three measure scholarly robustness.

Designers do not read the design implications sections of research papers. This system takes such a section and turns it out as a design card: a short title, a plain description, a generated illustration, a summary of the paper, the quoted evidence behind the claim, and the citation. Twenty-one designers rated cards against the original text, and twelve authors of the source papers judged whether the cards said what they had said. This card does not refilter the paper.

read to prove design operationalization · 3 PRELIMINARY STUDY: twelve designers shown mock-up cards built from three papers in several formats, saying which components they wanted, how much text, and what the evidence and citation should look like (PDF pp. 3–6); 4 DESIGN ITERATION AND IMPLEMENTATION: a two-sided card with the takeaway in front and the context behind, each component generated by a prompt, with the illustration drawn from the description (PDF pp. 6–7); 5.1 EVALUATION SETUP: twenty-one designers rating a card and the original text for two randomly assigned papers on six scales, and twelve authors judging the cards built from their own papers (PDF pp. 7–8); 5.3 QUANTITATIVE RESULTS: which format designers preferred, and how the two formats compared on inspirability, generativity, validity, generalizability, originality and actionability (PDF pp. 8–9); 5.4 QUALITATIVE RESULTS: what made the card easy to take in, what the image added, whether the authors recognised their own claim in it, and what they would want changed (PDF pp. 8–10)

The six borrowed criteria do the review's work for it, because they separate what moved from what did not. Inspirability rose significantly and generativity marginally, while validity, generalizability, originality and actionability all came out flat. Actionability is the criterion closest to whether a designer could do anything differently, and it is the one that did not budge, so the honest summary is that the card format made the same claim feel more stimulating without making it more usable. The authors present the four nulls as a success, that the card delivers the implication without sacrificing its validity, which is a fair reading for the three robustness criteria and a strained one for actionability. What the qualitative side shows is displacement of reading. The raw text was found harder to absorb and, in one designer's words, the card gave them the insight without having to read too much or decipher the source text. That is the point of a translational resource, and it is also the mechanism by which a reader stops checking: the evidence quote is on the card, so the paper need not be opened. Nobody in this study was asked to judge whether a generated card was faithful except the twelve authors of the source papers, who said it was, and no designer ever compared a card against the paper it came from.
